key_insight: Anchoring—regularizing independently trained predictors toward a common reference—controls and can drive down expected squared disagreement between models while preserving standard training workflows.
problem_solved: Reduces unpredictable model-to-model variation (disagreement) that arises when the same learning procedure is run on independent samples, improving consistency and trustworthiness of real-valued predictions.
method: Introduce an anchoring objective: add a penalty that pulls model parameters or predictions toward a shared anchor (e.g., an initial estimator or ensemble mean) during training.
Provide theoretical analysis linking anchor strength and data/sample properties to upper bounds on expected squared disagreement between independently trained models.
Empirically evaluate the trade-off between accuracy and agreement across datasets and show how tuning the anchoring parameter can reduce disagreement with minimal loss in predictive performance.
impact: Gives practitioners a simple, tunable mechanism to make models more consistent across retrainings or deployments, aiding reproducibility, fairness checks, and downstream system stability.
visual_elements: Schematic: two pipelines showing independent training vs. anchored training (arrow from anchor to both models).
Plot: disagreement (expected squared difference) on y-axis vs. anchoring strength on x-axis, with accuracy as a secondary curve.
Diagram: theoretical bound cartoon—anchor strength + sample size => disagreement upper bound.
Icon grid: use-cases (reproducibility, ensemble reduction, auditing, stable deployments) with short captions.
paper_authors: Eric Eaton, Surbhi Goel, Marcel Hussing, Michael Kearns, Aaron Roth
